Best cycling gloves 2026 reviewed

A quality pair of gloves are an essential to keep your hands warm and your fingers working when riding in the winter.

But, as Paul Seixas found when he crashed at the Tour Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes in 2026, even in the summer gloves are a valuable addition to your kit, providing protection for your hands. They’ll also soak up sweat and add some padding to prevent your hands from getting sore from grasping the handlebars and reduce the transmission of vibrations to your hands. Plus, gloves typically offer a wiping surface for sweat, snot, blood, insects or whatever.

We’ve rounded up our pick of the best summer cycling gloves and best winter cycling gloves, but you can also read our separate guides to each if you want more options. Plus, we have a guide to the best heated cycling gloves if your hands get really, really cold when riding.

Why trust Cyclist‘s advice?

At Cyclist, the weather doesn’t stop us riding, so come summer or winter we’ll be out reviewing the best road and gravel bikes and all the gear that goes with them. That means dressing for the conditions and an appropriate pair of gloves is as essential for a heatwave as for a bitter winter day. We know what to look for in a quality pair of gloves.

We’re not paid for our reviews or for product placement, so you can rely on Cyclist‘s reviewers to give you expert, unbiased advice.

The best summer cycling gloves reviewed

Altura Airstream mitts

£20 | Buy here

  • Pros: Comfortable fit, well placed padding, bonded cuff, price
  • Cons: Limited airflow, small snot wipe

Altura’s summer gloves are affordable and available in a wide range of sizes and colours. The palms include memory foam pads in their perforated synthetic suede, while the backs are made from high-wicking, stretchy fabric that conforms to your hands. There’s a bonded cuff seam that sits comfortably at the wrist and a tab on the underside to help get the gloves on and off.

We found the palm pads well placed to absorb road vibration. The smooth fabric does reduce airflow over a more open mesh though, so hands can get sweaty on hot days.

  • Read our full Altura Airstream mitts review

GripGrab Rouleur padded short finger gloves

£31 | Buy here

  • Pros: Comfortable fit, dense padding, good structure
  • Cons: S is the smallest size

GripGrab places the majority of its padding at the centre of the palm, with another pad between the thumb and index finger. The upper is thin enough for good airflow, despite not having perforations and the fit is close, without being tight, while the velcro tab at the cuff keeps the gloves in place well. Sizes available are S to XXL, although we reckon riders with smaller hands may find the S a little too large. The great fit and dense padding make for comfortable longer distance rides.

  • Read our full GripGrab Rouleur padding short finger gloves review

Le Col cycling mitts

£50 | Buy here

  • Pros: Compressive fit, stretchy fabric, comfortable cut
  • Cons: Awkward to get on and off, limited size range

Le Col’s mitts have a long cuff, which helps protect the base of the palm. Although only three sizes are available, the fabric on the backs is stretchy and compressive, so there’s a comfortably close fit, although the gloves may be too large for smaller hands. Along with their length, this does make them tricky to get on and off, though the fabric also offers enough ventilation to keep hands cool. Mesh between the fingers and a ventilated centre to the palm help too. The palm padding is well-placed and effective, but not too thick.

  • Read our full Le Col cycling mitts review

Sportful Matchy gloves

£39 | Buy here

  • Pros: Lots of colours and sizes, easy to get on and off
  • Cons: Not all sizes in all colours, thin padding

Sportful makes the Matchy gloves in men’s sizes from XS to XXL and women’s from XS to XL as well as a wide range of colours, although not all sizes are available in every colour. The fingers are quite long and the wrist is relatively loose, which helps get the gloves on and off. There’s a pad at the knuckles and another in the base of the palm, although these are both quite thin. They’re a better option for shorter rides in milder temperatures than long, hot excursions.

The best winter cycling gloves reviewed

Assos Ultraz Winter Gloves 

£105 | Buy here

  • Pros: Designed for deep winter riding in low temperatures, easy fit with pull-on neoprene cuffs
  • Cons: Showerproof but not waterproof

Assos achieves a great balance of warmth and easy on/off with the Ultraz Winter Gloves. They’re easy to remove when needed, but once on the Airblock windproof outer along with quality insulation and a fleece inner face keep hands warm down to zero or below. They’re good for cold, dry rides and the waterproofing will keep out showers but they will wet out on a ride in heavier rain.

  • Read our full Assos Ultraz Winter Gloves review

Café du Cycliste Classic gloves

£70 | Buy here

  • Pros: Comfortable, low bulk
  • Cons: Not designed for very cold temperatures, lack padding in the palms

If it’s not quite cold enough for the Assos Ultraz gloves, the Café du Cycliste Classic gloves might fit the bill. They’re not as thick, so dexterity is improved and there’s reinforcement of the palms at pressure points, although not quite enough to maintain comfort on longer rides. They’re a good option for the typical UK winter weather though.

  • Read our full Café du Cycliste Classic gloves review 

Castelli Perfetto RoS Gloves

£85 | Buy here

  • Pros: Cosy fleece lining, warm even when wet
  • Cons: Rated for use in milder temperatures between 4° and 14°C, tricky to get on once wet

Another option for milder autumn/spring days, Castelli’s gloves offer windproofing and breathability without too much bulk, thanks to a single Gore-Tex Windstopper fabric layer without extra insulation beyond the fleece backing. The neoprene cuff keeps the weather out, but makes the gloves awkward to remove and replace when wet.

  • Read our full Castelli Perfetto RoS Gloves review

Rapha Winter Gloves 

£85 | Buy here

  • Pros: Well insulated, stylish design, generous faux suede nose wipe
  • Cons: Tend to become sweaty at milder temperatures

Rapha’s gloves are less basic than their chunky looks suggest and provide plenty of warmth as the temperature approaches zero. They keep the rain out well and dry out quickly too, although this does lead to a tendency to get sweaty inside when its a little bit warmer. They’re easier to get off and on than many competitor products and the suede palm offers plenty of grip.

  • Read our full Rapha Winter Gloves review

Velocio Zero winter gloves

£93 | Buy here

  • Pros: Very warm, robust strap, good waterproofing
  • Cons: Difficult to manipulate controls, don’t work with touchscreens

Velocio’s three-layer weather protection includes a wind blocking microfleece made by seat pad supremos Elastic Interface, which extends to the palms, with the backs including Primaloft insulation under a weatherproof outer layer. A wide velcro strap at the wrist ensures a secure closure.

The Zero gloves are Velocio’s best insulated, so they’re warm down towards zero. They can get sweaty when it’s milder though and their bulk does impact dexterity. There’s some water ingress on longer, wet rides, but they’re fine for showers, although more geared to cold, dry excursions. We found it impossible to operate a touchscreen without removing a glove.

How do I choose the best cycling gloves for me?

Protection

Summer or winter, a primary function of cycling gloves is to provide protection for your hands, both from discomfort from the handlebars and in the event of a crash. For the latter, some gloves are made of abrasion-resistant fabrics. Protection from the bars may come in the form of a thicker fabric, while many gloves include foam or gel inserts to distribute the load.

Fit and adjustment

To be comfortable, a cycling glove should fit relatively closely, or you’ll substitute rubbing against your gloves for rubbing on your handlebars. Many gloves include a velcro tab at the wrist for adjustment, although others rely on elastic or, in the summer, the fabric’s stretch to keep them in place.

Fabrics

The fabric choice for winter gloves is obviously going to be very different from that for summer mitts. In the winter, look for windproofing, rain resistance and quality insulation. Winter gloves will often have a waterproof membrane built into their uppers. The palms need to be relatively thin still to preserve your bar feel and allow you to work the bike’s controls, although this will result in less weather protection.

In the summer, the upper fabric needs to do the opposite and keep you cool, so it’s usually a lightweight fabric or mesh, although a crocheted upper will give summer mitts a retro feel. The palm will be thinner too, although it’s still useful to have some padding and isolation from the handlebars. Leather has been a popular material for glove palms, although it’s now usually synthetic.

Aerodynamics

As with everything cycling, you can choose aero gloves that are claimed to help you to go faster. In general, aero gloves have a longer cuff that stretches well above the wrist. They’re usually made of smooth fabrics and without logos or closures which might cause extra drag.
